passage: Yusuf, five, went with his aunt Reena to meet her old teacher. At the door Reena said, "Namaste, ma'am," with folded hands. Yusuf copied her, then bent down and touched the teacher's feet. She laughed kindly. "Namaste is plenty, beta. In our house we just fold hands." Yusuf glanced up at Reena, unsure. Reena whispered, "That was lovely. Every family does it a little differently."

qa.q: What two things did Yusuf do to greet the teacher?
qa.a: He folded his hands and then bent down to touch her feet.

qa.q: What might Yusuf be worried about after the teacher laughed?
qa.a: Whether he had done it wrong. His glance suggests he was unsure, though he might also have been checking that she approved.

qa.q: What could Reena say later to help Yusuf feel safe about greetings?
qa.a: Tell him kindly that families greet differently and that he was being respectful, and show him the way this teacher prefers.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Yusuf's gesture?
qa.a: As a sweet sign of respect. She laughed kindly rather than correcting him sharply, even though her own custom is to fold hands. 🙂

grounding: Shows a child greeting elders with namaste and feet-touching, with customs differing and the child taught kindly.

passage:
"Rafiq, Nani is here. Go and say salaam."
"Do I touch her feet?"
"Who told you that?"
"Aarav does, at school."
"Some families do, some don't. In ours we say salaam, and a hug if Nani wants one."
"What if I forget?"
"Then Nani will smile and you say it again."
Rafiq's mother Vinita gave him a small nudge. He walked over, said, "Salaam, Nani," and waited. Nani opened her arms.

qa.q: Who does Rafiq say touches feet at school?
qa.a: Aarav.

qa.q: What was Rafiq worried about when he asked, "What if I forget?"
qa.a: Getting the greeting wrong in front of Nani. He may also simply have wanted reassurance from his mother.

qa.q: How did Vinita handle Rafiq's question kindly?
qa.a: She explained that families differ and told him forgetting is fine, instead of scolding him.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Rafiq says salaam and waits?
qa.a: Likely touched and welcoming, since she opened her arms. She might equally have been glad to see him however he greeted her.

grounding: Shows a child unsure whether to touch elders' feet or say salaam, taught kindly that customs vary.

passage:
Grandparents' Day note, from Suraj, KG teacher.
Today several children touched their grandparents' feet when they arrived. Zubin stood still, unsure, while his grandmother waited. A boy said, “Why didn't you touch her feet? That's rude!” Zubin's face went red. I said, “Families greet in different ways. Some touch feet, some say namaste, some hug, some say salaam.” Zubin's grandmother opened her arms, and Zubin ran into a hug. Later the class shared how each family greets elders.

qa.q: What did some children do when their grandparents arrived?
qa.a: They touched their grandparents' feet.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when his face went red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed when the boy called him rude, and unsure what he was supposed to do.

qa.q: How did Suraj respond to the boy's comment?
qa.a: Suraj explained kindly that families greet in different ways, so Zubin was not shamed.

qa.q: How might the boy who said “rude” see greetings after the class sharing?
qa.a: He might learn that there are many respectful ways to greet elders, not only the one his family uses.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a child unsure how to greet an elder, and the teacher explaining that customs vary rather than shaming him.

passage: Zainab went home with her friend after school, in their small town. Her friend's Dadi was on the porch, and her friend bent down and touched Dadi's feet. Zainab stood holding her bag, not sure what to do. Swati, her friend's mother, noticed. “Zainab, beta, you can greet Dadi however your family does.” Zainab thought. “At home I say adaab.” She raised her hand to her forehead. “Adaab, Dadi.” Dadi smiled and did the same back. “Adaab, beti. Come, have some sherbet.”

qa.q: How did Zainab greet Dadi?
qa.a: She raised her hand to her forehead and said, “Adaab, Dadi.”

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling as she stood holding her bag?
qa.a: She was unsure and a little nervous about how to greet Dadi, since her friend's custom was different from hers.

qa.q: What did Swati say that helped?
qa.a: She told Zainab she could greet Dadi however her family does, so Zainab didn't feel she had to copy.

qa.q: How might Dadi see Zainab's adaab?
qa.a: She took it as a warm, respectful greeting and returned it, showing respect across customs.

grounding: A child unsure of another family's custom is taught kindly that she can greet the elder in her own family's way.

passage: At her friend Priyanka's Diwali party in Johannesburg, Zanele watched Priyanka bend and touch her grandfather's feet. Zanele wanted to do it too. She bent down awkwardly and touched his shoes. Everyone laughed, and her cheeks burned. Priyanka's grandfather laughed too, but kindly, and lifted her up by the hands. “Thank you, child. That was very respectful. A handshake is lovely too.” He shook her hand. Her father, Anders, winked at her from the doorway, and her shoulders relaxed.

qa.q: Whose party was Zanele at?
qa.a: Her friend Priyanka's Diwali party.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when her cheeks burned?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed when everyone laughed, worried she had done it wrong.

qa.q: What did Priyanka's grandfather do that taught kindly?
qa.a: He thanked her, called it respectful, and offered a handshake as another way, so she did not feel shamed.

qa.q: What would change if the grandfather had said “That's not how you do it”?
qa.a: Zanele might feel ashamed and avoid trying new customs again.

grounding: A child tries touching an elder's feet at a friend's party and is taught kindly that another greeting is fine too.

passage:
At the school's annual day, the chief guest, an elderly former headmaster, sat by the stage. One by one, children bent down and touched his feet.

When Aditi's turn came, she froze. At home her family simply folded their hands. She stood there, hands half-raised.

"You didn't touch his feet!" a classmate hissed.

Tejas Sir walked over and crouched beside her. "Families greet in different ways. Some touch feet, some say namaste, some just smile. Which one do you know?"

Aditi folded her hands. "Namaste."

The old man smiled and folded his hands back.

qa.q: What did children do one by one when greeting the chief guest?
qa.a: They bent down and touched his feet.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she froze with her hands half-raised?
qa.a: She was most likely unsure and a little anxious, because her family greets with folded hands and everyone else was touching feet. The classmate's hiss probably made her feel embarrassed too.

qa.q: How did Tejas Sir help Aditi without shaming her?
qa.a: He explained that families greet in different ways and let her choose the greeting she knew, so she could show respect in her own way.

qa.q: How does the chief guest respond to Aditi's namaste?
qa.a: He smiles and folds his hands back, showing he accepts her greeting as respectful.

grounding: It shows a child unsure whether to touch an elder's feet or say namaste, and a teacher kindly explaining that customs vary rather than shaming her.
